newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Safeway joins BP in food and fuel stores.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Safeway joins BP in food and fuel stores.

text.p: Britain's Safeway supermarkets and British Petroleum joined forces on Friday to launch "food and fuel" stores, promising 100 million pounds ($156.6 million) of investments and 2,000 jobs if the format wins favour.
Safeway and BP said the 50-50 venture aimed to develop 100 sites to sell food and petrol throughout the UK.
The sites will be picked from BP's existing network of over 2,000 service stations created by the merger of BP and Mobil's European retail business.
"We believe there is a rapidly growing demand for this style of combined retail outlet," Rolf Stomberg, chief executive of BP Oil, said in a statement.
Safeways' communications director Kevin Hawkins said refurbishment of each outlet would cost about one million pounds and the entire project could mean creation of over 2,000 new jobs.

The cooperation between the two companies is in sharp contrast to the backdrop of a current fierce price war on petrol between supermarkets and oil majors, which has slashed profits and squeezed margins.
"Price wars come and go, we are looking here at a long-term investment," said Hawkins.
He said Safeway expected higher value sales in the food and fuel outlets than in its supermarkets, where levels are just over 14 pounds per square foot, including petrol.
Gross margins, meanwhile, should be about the same, he said.
Analysts were divided on the benefits of the move, with some seeing little impact on Safeway's profits while at least one felt it may add 20 million pounds or so at the operating level.
"It is a question of whether two plus two can ever equally very much more than four," said one sector analyst who asked not to be named.
Shares in Safeway mirrored the muted reaction, adding just 1/2 pence to 329-1/2 pence in late morning trade while BP was down 1/2 pence at 625.
"It is a very neat idea but the actual impact on profits could be negligible," the sector analyst said.
Bill Myers at Williams de Broe highlighted the speed with which Safeway and BP should be able to put the plan into practice, as the sites are already on the map.
"The real beauty (of the deal) is in comparing the numbers. There are 2,000 existing sites from which they can cherry-pick just 100," said Myers.
Safeway's Hawkins said the company hoped development would be hastened because the sites were already owned by BP.
"Assuming the test sites perform well and planning permission is gained, there should be a rapid rollout," he said, with most of the planned stores up and running in 2-3 years.
But it will be up to customers to give the new format the green light and the go-ahead, with its success based on "customer reaction and sales...the acid test," Hawkins said.
The format, which includes car washes and cashpoint banking machines, aims to target not just convenience shopping for snacks but to provide food for everyday meals.
Outlets will have dedicated parking for cars, but will also have a separate pedestrian access, Safeway said, and should make shopping easier and more convenient for customers.
"The idea is similar to Tesco's Express format, but there are only eight of those and six planned for next year," one analyst said. ($1=.6385 Pound)
